video:video.video:title: How to build an MMORPG from scratch in C++ | Building nanoMMO #1
video:video.video:description: In this first episode, we start building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, and the series is going to focus on the engineering around the game: Docker, CI, benchmarking, Prometheus and Grafana, MySQL, Redis and profiling. We sketch the architecture, and then set up a C++20 project written to Google's style guide, with CMake, GoogleTest, a Docker build, and GitHub Actions checking the style.

video:video.video:title: C++ game client with raylib, ImGui and shaders | Building nanoMMO
video:video.video:description: We start the C++ client of our MMORPG with raylib, a frame loop and Dear ImGui, and test the renderer in Docker on a virtual display, as there's no screen there to open a window on. Then we set up a 3D camera, write our first GLSL shaders to light a cube for our character, and move it around a ground of tiles. This is episode 2 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: C++ multiplayer with protobuf and Asio | Building nanoMMO
video:video.video:description: We start the multiplayer server, with a contract between client and server in protobuf, messages framed over TCP, and Asio accepting the clients. The world lives on the server, with tests, and several clients see each other's cubes move. We also go over why we start with TCP, when UDP is the better choice, and how Asio lets us switch later. This is episode 3 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: Prometheus and Grafana for a C++ game server | Building nanoMMO
video:video.video:description: We add metrics to our C++ game server with prometheus-cpp, and write bots that play like someone at the keys. Docker Compose runs the server, Prometheus and Grafana together, with the dashboard set up from files in the repo, and with three hundred bots online we see the bytes we send grow much faster than the players. This is episode 4 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: C++ game accounts with MySQL and Argon2id | Building nanoMMO
video:video.video:description: We give our players accounts, with MySQL in Docker Compose and passwords hashed with Argon2id through libsodium, talking to MySQL from C++ through its C API and prepared statements. Along the way we go over SQL or NoSQL, salts and slow hashes, SQL injection, and integration tests against MySQL in a container, in CI too. This is episode 5 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: C++ login server with Redis tokens | Building nanoMMO
video:video.video:description: We let our players log in, through a login server that checks passwords away from the game's tick, and hands each login over as a one-time token in Redis. The game server loads the player with it and saves where they are, so you come back where you left off, and the client gets a login screen. This is episode 6 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: raylib 3D animation in C++ with Mixamo and glTF | Building nanoMMO
video:video.video:description: We turn our cubes into 3D characters with skeletal animation in raylib, from Mixamo's X Bot and Y Bot, converted from FBX to glTF in Docker. Loading them as they come doesn't work, so a small glTF tool fixes their skins and bones, and the client blends the clips and skins the characters on the GPU. This is episode 7 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: Profiling a C++ game server with perf and Tracy | Building nanoMMO
video:video.video:description: We benchmark our C++ game server to see how many players it can take, and it falls behind past a thousand. Profiling it under load with perf and Tracy points at the broadcast, which serialised the whole world for each client, so we serialise it once a tick, and the server keeps up with twice the players. This is episode 8 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: TCP vs UDP for a game server, under packet loss | Building nanoMMO
video:video.video:description: We compare TCP and UDP for our game server under packet loss, with netem dropping a share of the packets and our bots measuring how old their newest world is. Over TCP, head-of-line blocking makes the worlds wait for each lost packet, so we send the world over UDP, in parts that fit in a packet, and make that the default. This is episode 9 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: C++ MMO monsters with AI, health and levels | Building nanoMMO
video:video.video:description: We add the first monsters to our world, a skeleton from Quaternius that the client loads as it is, with a wander AI that the server runs each tick. Players and monsters get health and levels, and players get experience, saved in MySQL and shown with health bars over everyone. This is episode 10 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: C++ MMO combat with swords, hits and respawns | Building nanoMMO
video:video.video:description: We add combat, so our players can fight the monsters from episode ten with a sword in their hand. The space bar swings it, the server decides what it hits and who gets the experience, and the monsters run at players near their home, swing back, and respawn after they die. This is episode 11 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: Laravel game website in Docker, with login and rankings | Building nanoMMO
video:video.video:description: We build a website for our game with Laravel, running on FrankenPHP in our Docker Compose stack, with a front page that ranks the players by experience. You can create an account and log in there too, with passwords hashed the way the login server does it, so an account made on the website works in the game as well. This is episode 12 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: Redis cache in C++ with write-behind to MySQL | Building nanoMMO
video:video.video:description: We stop our players losing their progress when the C++ game server crashes. Saving to MySQL after each tick falls behind at fifty players, so we put Redis in between, written in a single round trip each tick, and a saver of our own writes behind to MySQL. Then we crash the server, and the players come back where they were. This is episode 13 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: TLS for a C++ game server with OpenSSL and Asio | Building nanoMMO
video:video.video:description: We put TLS 1.3 on each TCP connection in our game, after watching passwords and tokens cross the network in plain text with tcpdump. We go through the handshake and certificates, make a certificate authority of our own, bring in OpenSSL through Asio's SSL stream, and check what it costs. This is episode 14 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: Procedural terrain in C++ with noise and raylib | Building nanoMMO
video:video.video:description: We replace our board of tiles with a procedural island, 512 metres across, from value noise and a seed that the server and the client share. Both have to compute the island to the last bit, so we turn off fused multiply-adds and pin a fingerprint in a test, and the client draws it low-poly, with a sea, fog and a camera that follows you. This is episode 15 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: Trees and frustum culling in C++ with raylib | Building nanoMMO
video:video.video:description: We grow trees on our island where the seed says, from a low-poly model under CC BY, with trunks the server makes solid. Then we measure how fast the client draws it all, with a benchmark of its own, and make it a lot faster by splitting the island into chunks and drawing the ones the camera can see. This is episode 16 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: Game character screen in C++ with raylib, ImGui | Building nanoMMO
video:video.video:description: We build a character screen with your name, level, health, experience and position, next to an idle model of your character. The client draws the model into a render texture through a camera of its own, Dear ImGui shows it in a window, and a test checks the preview on a hidden window. This is episode 17 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: MySQL schema migrations with Flyway in Docker | Building nanoMMO
video:video.video:description: We bring in Flyway to keep our MySQL tables in versioned migrations, so that changing a table no longer means deleting the database and its accounts. Docker Compose runs it before the servers, and then we save the players' health, where an edited first migration fails its checksum and the change gets a second migration instead. This is episode 18 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: Deploy a C++ game server to a VPS with Docker | Building nanoMMO
video:video.video:description: We deploy our game to a VPS on the internet, a DreamHost one with two virtual CPUs (the affiliate link is below). We decide what the internet gets to reach, write a production compose file and a deploy script that builds a commit on the server, and put the VPS under load with our bots. This is episode 19 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: MMO interest management to send each player less | Building nanoMMO
video:video.video:description: We cut what our server sends each player with interest management, as sending everyone the whole world grows with the square of the players. Our bots take trips so that they spread out, the island goes into cells of 32 metres, and each player gets what's near them, measured on my machine and on the VPS. This is episode 20 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: Consul service discovery for a C++ game server | Building nanoMMO
video:video.video:description: We run several worlds instead of one, each registered with Consul through its HTTP API, with a heartbeat so that a world that crashes drops out of the list. The login server lists the healthy worlds, you pick one before you log in, Prometheus finds them through Consul too, and each world gets its own players. This is episode 21 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: MMO zones and portals in C++ with raylib | Building nanoMMO
video:video.video:description: We give each world a second land, the Ashlands, with a gate between it and the Meadows, the way MMOs have zones. The look of a land becomes data that the shaders read each frame, the world server runs both lands in one process, and a Flyway migration keeps the land a player is in. This is episode 22 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: MMO chat in C++ with TCP, ImGui and rate limits | Building nanoMMO
video:video.video:description: We add a chat to our MMO, where a line goes to everyone in your world, over TCP even for the clients that get the world over UDP. The client gets a chat window in ImGui, the server cleans each line and a token bucket keeps anyone from flooding it, and our bots chat now and then too. This is episode 23 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: Data-driven MMO NPCs in C++ on low bandwidth | Building nanoMMO
video:video.video:description: We add NPCs to our world, a guard, a merchant and a healer in each land, after turning our monsters into data. NPCs don't move, so the server puts them into their interest cells once and sends them once a second, and the client keeps each one for a few seconds, so that a lost datagram doesn't make them blink. This is episode 24 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: An LLM-powered NPC in a C++ MMO server | Building nanoMMO
video:video.video:description: We give one of our NPCs a language model: a storyteller that writes you a story from a few words, with mvGPT from my other series running next to the game. The server asks it from threads of its own, so that the tick doesn't wait for a story, and the client picks the NPC with a ray from the mouse. This is episode 25 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: MMO items in C++ with protobuf text format | Building nanoMMO
video:video.video:description: We start an item system with the sword our players hold, moving its reach, damage and look into an items file in protobuf's text format, which the server and the client both read. A parser refuses a misspelt field, and each player holds a weapon by its id, saved in Redis and MySQL. This is episode 26 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: Data-driven MMO content in C++ with protobuf | Building nanoMMO
video:video.video:description: We turn the rest of our game's content into data, with the kinds of monsters and NPCs, and where they stand, in a content folder that both sides read. Monsters and NPCs go out by their kind's id, a hash of the content keeps clients off worlds they don't match, and a new monster joins without a line of code. This is episode 27 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: C++ sanitizers, fuzzing and coverage in Docker | Building nanoMMO
video:video.video:description: We look for the bugs our tests don't find, with AddressSanitizer, UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer and ThreadSanitizer while two hundred bots play, a fuzzer, clang-tidy and a coverage report. They find a leak in raylib, a data race in our metrics' web server and stories the storyteller would lose, and we fix what they find, in Docker and in CI. This is episode 28 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: Integration testing a C++ game server | Building nanoMMO
video:video.video:description: We write an integration test for our C++ game server, which starts a world server inside the test, against MySQL and Redis, and has players join it over TLS like the client does. The test waits for what it checks without sleeping, the sanitisers catch a bug in the test, and the coverage report shows how much more of the server we test now. This is episode 29 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: Prometheus Alertmanager alert rules and email | Building nanoMMO
video:video.video:description: We have Prometheus alert us on what players would notice, a world that falls behind and a world that crashes, and watch the alerts go pending and fire. A crashed world drops out of Consul and lets go of its alert, so we write a rule that holds on, and Alertmanager emails each alert to Mailpit, with promtool testing the rules in CI. This is episode 30 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: MMORPG skills, cooldowns and a hotbar in C++ | Building nanoMMO
video:video.video:description: We give our players skills, a thrust, a kick, a whirlwind and second wind, as content that the server decides, with a level to reach and a cooldown. The client gets a hotbar on the number keys with icons and countdowns, the characters get new animations from Mixamo, and the camera learns to tilt. This is episode 31 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: Game music in C++ with raylib audio | Building nanoMMO
video:video.video:description: We add music to our MMORPG with raylib's audio, from a track streamed off its file that turns out to need refilling each frame. A jukebox fades it in and out and rests between plays, and the settings get volume sliders in decibels, kept in a file written so that a crash leaves the old one whole. Music by Pavel Bekirov, from Pixabay. This is episode 32 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: Bloom and cel shading in C++ with raylib | Building nanoMMO
video:video.video:description: We add post-processing to our MMORPG's client with raylib, starting from its bloom example, which washes the whole world out. So we build bloom from what's brighter than white, have the lava and second wind give off light, and then add cel shading with flat bands and outlines, and FXAA to smooth the edges. This is episode 33 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: MMORPG skill trainer NPC with MySQL and Redis | Building nanoMMO
video:video.video:description: We fix why CI has failed since episode 28, and then add a skill trainer, an NPC who teaches you a skill once you reach its level. The server checks each lesson, where a test catches the level we forgot, the client gets a window to learn in, and what players learn is saved through Redis to MySQL. This is episode 34 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: Game server logs with Grafana Loki and Alloy | Building nanoMMO
video:video.video:description: We keep our servers' logs in Grafana Loki, with Grafana Alloy reading each container's output from Docker, where a component we forgot to wire up files all the lines under one name. We label the lines by service and stream, put the errors on the dashboard next to the metrics, and have Loki alert us when the saver can't reach MySQL. This is episode 35 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: Zero downtime deploys for an MMORPG game server | Building nanoMMO
video:video.video:description: We deploy new versions of our worlds without throwing anyone out, by having a world hand its players over to its next instance through Consul before it stops. Each move needs a fresh token, as we find out when a reused one sends alice back to the login screen, and handover.sh restarts a world this way while forty bots play on. This is episode 36 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: Deploy on push with a self-hosted GitHub Actions runner | Building nanoMMO
video:video.video:description: We have our VPS deploy each push to main on its own, once CI passes, with a self-hosted GitHub Actions runner in Docker. The runner reaches the server's Docker through its socket, works in the deploying user's home folder at the path it has on the server, and starts each release through the worlds' next instances, so the players play on. As our repository is public, the runner refuses any job but a deploy of main. This is episode 37 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: Instanced dungeons for an MMORPG game server | Building nanoMMO
video:video.video:description: We give each player who walks into a dungeon a copy of it of their own, the way MMORPGs instance their dungeons. The world server runs its lands as copies, the gates get a list of their own, and the Crypt, our first dungeon, gets a copy for each player who goes in, with its own skeletons. The nanommo_copies metric shows that the copies stay after forty bots leave, so a copy nobody's in stops, and goes after five minutes, and players in the Crypt are saved outside it, so that a logout or a deploy brings them back to the Meadows. This is episode 38 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: A data-driven item system for an MMO game server | Building nanoMMO
video:video.video:description: We design the item system of our MMORPG as data: an item is the parts it has, such as how many stack, where it's worn and what it adds, what using one does and what each one rolls, instead of a type in the code, and the content's checks refuse parts that don't go together. Then a bag of twenty-four slots, with a slot for each piece of equipment, which stacks, splits, swaps and wears items, and a property test that makes twenty thousand random moves and checks that no item is ever made or lost. This is episode 39 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: Saving MMO inventories with Redis and MySQL | Building nanoMMO
video:video.video:description: We give each player of our MMORPG a bag to carry, and save it. A new player gets their kit once, what they wear adds to their damage, health and armour, and a potion from the bag heals them, with a cooldown of its own. Then the bags are saved through Redis to MySQL, a row for each stack, only when they change, in a transaction, and in statements small enough for MySQL to take five hundred full bags at once. This is episode 40 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: Drag and drop MMORPG inventory with Dear ImGui | Building nanoMMO
video:video.video:description: We put our MMORPG's inventory on screen. The server sends each player their bag over TCP when it changes, and takes what they do with it, moving, wearing, drinking and throwing away, with a rate limit and refusals in words. The client draws the bag in a window with Dear ImGui and raylib, each item's icon in its tint, with tooltips, drag and drop, and a row in the character window for what's worn, and the windows draw the bag the server sent, so what you see is what the server decided. This is episode 41 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: MMORPG loot tables and drops on a C++ server | Building nanoMMO
video:video.video:description: We give our MMORPG's monsters loot tables. Each kind of monster lists the items it can drop, each with a chance and how many, and when it dies, the server rolls them and puts what drops into its killer's bag, a stack at a time or one at a time with rolls of their own, and the chat says what dropped, or what didn't fit. The content's checks refuse loot that doesn't add up, the bots drink potions and wear what they find, and the world fuzzer moves items to any place a client could send. This is episode 42 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: Low poly water shader for an MMORPG in C++ | Building nanoMMO
video:video.video:description: We give our MMORPG's sea waves with raylib and GLSL, trying three ways: ripples in the light on a flat sea, smooth waves that move a grid of triangles in the vertex shader, and flat-shaded facets, each triangle lit by its face's normal from dFdx and dFdy, which match our low poly world. Then the sea reads the ground's heights from a texture, so it calms down and foams at the shore, and each land gets a liquid of its own: water, lava that glows at the tops of its waves, and a green ooze. This is episode 43 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: Low poly characters for an MMORPG in C++ | Building nanoMMO
video:video.video:description: We replace our MMORPG's Mixamo characters with low poly people, made of parts that a protocol buffer file describes: limbs with round ends and balls, each bound to one bone of the bots' skeletons with raylib's GPU skinning, so their animations still pose them. First a look at what we tried in a lab, people in clothes, one-colour stick figures, a skeleton and a spider with inverse kinematics, and why we kept the people. Each player gets a skin and a way to wear their hair from their id, the outline gets a hull with smooth normals, the server sends what each player wears, and an item's look gets parts of its own. A new player starts in a shirt of their own colour, trousers and shoes, which are items, so the leather cap, tunic, boots and buckler show on whoever wears them too, with a shadow under each figure. This is episode 44 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: MMORPG quest system in C++, with NPCs that give quests | Building nanoMMO
video:video.video:description: We add quests to our MMORPG: a quest is data, in a protocol buffer file, with the NPC who gives it, how many of which monster it asks you to kill, and the experience and items it gives. The server decides it all: taking a quest from its giver, counting the kills for it, and turning it in for its reward, with the prizes going into a copy of the bag first, so that it's all of them or none. The client gets its quests over TCP, like its bag, with a quest window, a tracker in the corner, and a gold mark over each NPC with a quest for you. The quests are saved as JSON in the player's row in MySQL, through Redis, and the world fuzzer takes and turns them in too. Before that, the NPCs become low poly people, like the players, and we fix what CI found in the last episode's code, with clang-format and clang-tidy. This is episode 45 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: MMORPG server load test, with flame graphs from Pyroscope | Building nanoMMO
video:video.video:description: We load test our MMORPG's server again, twenty-six episodes after the last time, with bots that do what players do now: they take quests from the NPCs, hunt the monsters the quests ask for, and turn them in. And this time, the server is profiled all the time, with Grafana's Pyroscope: Alloy samples our C++ servers from the kernel with eBPF, with no change to their code, and Grafana shows a flame graph of where the worlds spend their CPU, under their metrics and logs. Then two thousand bots, and what the flame graph shows at the limit, from the broadcast to the kernel's UDP stack. This is episode 46 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: MMORPG game analytics with ClickHouse and Grafana | Building nanoMMO
video:video.video:description: We add game analytics to our MMORPG: each kill, drop, quest taken and turned in, level reached, potion drunk and death is an event, recorded by the world on the C++ server. Once a tick, the server adds them to a Redis stream, so the game never waits on the analytics, and a recorder takes them from there, as a consumer group, in batches, into ClickHouse, a column-oriented database that counts millions of rows quickly. Then a Grafana dashboard of the game, from ClickHouse: kills a minute, the quests taken against the ones done, the items that come into the game against the ones used, and where players die. This is episode 47 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: Recap and what's next | Building nanoMMO
video:video.video:description: A check-in, with no code this time: a look back over the forty-seven episodes so far, from a C++ server and a raylib client to quests, a load test with Pyroscope and analytics in ClickHouse. We go over how the game fits together today, play it, and look at the tools around it, the dashboards and CI, and the practices from the industry we've put in place. Then the plan: more of the features you'd expect in an MMORPG, more worlds and graphics, a trading system, all the players simulated by bots, and more on security. This is episode 48 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: MMORPG game events with an event queue in C++ | Building nanoMMO
video:video.video:description: We give our MMORPG game events, sent from the C++ server to the clients: an event queue, as Robert Nystrom's Game Programming Patterns calls it, where the world records what happens, and the server decides who reads it. The world records each hit, each blow taken and the health given back as events, next to the kills, levels and the rest it records for the analytics, which leave them out. The protocol gets an event message, and each tick the server sends each player the events near them, in their copy of the land, through the interest management's cells, over TCP so that none are lost, while the world's state goes on over UDP. The client keeps the events apart from the world it draws, and shows each as combat text: the damage over the monster, what it does back in red, healing in green, and a new level in gold. Along the way, a dead monster loses its nameplate, and the bots stop swinging at a body. This is episode 49 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: MMORPG loading screen and death screen in C++ | Building nanoMMO
video:video.video:description: Our MMORPG gets a loading screen and a death screen. Entering a world, or going through a gate, the raylib client covers the world in the land's sky, with its name, until the land is built, and waits for a frame of the cover to be on the screen before it does anything that holds a frame up. Then the fog lifts off the new land, nearest first, so that it comes out of its sky instead of appearing all at once. On the C++ server, the dead now come back when they ask to, once their wait is over, and each world tells them how long they have left, which the client counts down to a Respawn button. The bots come back as soon as they can. And the gates get round platforms, in a ring of pointed stones. This is episode 50 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: MMORPG click targeting in C++ to pick a monster, run up and attack | Building nanoMMO
video:video.video:description: Our MMORPG's fights go for the monster you pick now, not whatever's nearest. The C++ server keeps each player's pick from their input, and swings and skills that hit one monster go for it. In the raylib client, a click on a monster picks it, with a red ring at its feet and a frame beside yours, and the hotbar shows which skills need a pick. The cursor turns into a hand over someone you can talk to, and a crosshair over a monster, and an NPC answers a click only from within talking reach. And a swing or a skill at a monster out of reach runs you up to it first, on the server. This is episode 51 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: MMORPG pathfinding in C++ with A*, a map and a minimap | Building nanoMMO
video:video.video:description: Our MMORPG gets pathfinding. The C++ server marks each metre square of a land a player can walk on, and finds the way around trees, lakes and lava with A*: a priority queue ordered by the cost so far plus the octile distance left, a cap on how much it searches, and a way straightened to the places where it turns. A search across the island takes about a quarter of a millisecond. A double click on the ground, or a click on the new map, walks you there by yourself. The raylib client draws each land from above into a texture for the map on M and the minimap in the corner, and the monster camps spread over the land, at least thirty metres apart. This is episode 52 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: MMORPG skill animation and VFX in C++ with keyframes, trails and sparks | Building nanoMMO
video:video.video:description: Our MMORPG's skills move the way we write them now, not the way a downloaded clip does. A skill's move is a few keys in the content, each turning a handful of joints at a time into the skill, with an ease that makes a strike snap and a wind-up gather. The raylib client turns the bones on top of the standing clip, each joint taking the bones below it round, and works out the GPU's skinning matrices again. Then come the fx: a trail where the sword has just been, posed again at moments just gone, glows, rings along the ground, sparks, motes and a camera shake, each worked out from the time since the skill started, so it looks alike at any frame rate. The C++ server sends the monster a skill lands on, and the swing on Space becomes Strike, a skill every player has, with the weapon's reach, damage and timing. This is episode 53 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: MMORPG skill effects in C++ for stone, ice, lightning and fire | Building nanoMMO
video:video.video:description: Our MMORPG gets four new skills, each a move of its own and a list of fx in the skills file. The raylib client draws shards thrown up from the ground and spikes of stone and ice that come up nearest first, as solid gems lit by the world's shader, then lightning that finds a new path each flicker, and a crescent of fire that flies forward from the player. The C++ server gets an arc, so a skill can hit a slice in front of the player and nothing behind. Earthsplitter, Frost Nova, Searing Arc and Stormcaller are entries in a text file, on top of last episode's moves and fx. This is episode 54 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: MMORPG footstep sounds made from code in C++ | Building nanoMMO
video:video.video:description: Our MMORPG gets its first sound effects, and the raylib client makes them from numbers as it starts, without a single sound file. We build a small synthesizer in C++: noise, a state variable filter, sine waves and envelopes. From those come footsteps for grass, sand, rock, snow, ash, stone and water, in takes that don't repeat back to back, timed to the frames where the walk puts each foot down, and heard by distance and side. A small tool of our own plays each sound outside the game. This is episode 55 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: MMORPG skill and gate sounds made from code in C++ | Building nanoMMO
video:video.video:description: Our MMORPG's skills get their sounds, made by the raylib client from numbers, without a single sound file. Each kind of fx a skill lists, from a trail to lightning, has a sound of its own, built from noise, tones and filters, with a cold colour ringing higher than a warm one, so a new skill built from them comes with its sound. Going through a gate rises two octaves as the world fades, and each land greets us with a chord: major, minor or diminished. This is episode 56 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: MMORPG trailer from code in C++ with slow motion, a sky and clouds | Building nanoMMO
video:video.video:description: Our MMORPG films its own trailer: a cinema tool draws each shot through the raylib client's own renderer a frame at a time, so the game's clock can run five times slower than the film's, at 4K on any screen. We give the game a sky, with a sun and low-poly clouds whose shadows drift over the land, write a stage where players use their skills and monsters fall to them, mix the game's sounds into each shot, and film the trailer. This is episode 57 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: MMO character selection in C++ with a 3D preview | Building nanoMMO
video:video.video:description: Our MMORPG's accounts get characters of their own now. MySQL keeps each character with an id and a name, up to four of them in each world, and a migration turns the players we had into the first characters. The C++ login server answers a login with a session, which stands in for the password from then on, lists the account's characters, makes and deletes them, and gives a token to enter a world as one. In the raylib client, the login comes first, then the worlds, then your characters, each drawn in 3D as it looks, turned with the mouse. This is episode 58 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: Versioning a C++ MMO and updating its libraries | Building nanoMMO
video:video.video:description: Our MMORPG gets a version, set once in CMake for the C++ client and all the servers: the client shows it in the corner of its login screen, the servers print it as they start, and Prometheus gets it as a build info metric. The login server checks each client's version and turns away one that doesn't speak its protocol, saying which version to get. A Python script lists the C++ libraries FetchContent pins that have newer versions, moves them on and pins each by its SHA-256, and when raylib 6.2 breaks our tests with a double free, we see why updates go through CI. Dependabot and a GitHub Actions workflow open pull requests with the newest versions each week, and a changelog says what each version changed. This is episode 59 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: Procedural walk and run cycles with two-bone IK in a C++ MMORPG | Building nanoMMO
video:video.video:description: Our MMORPG's people stand on a skeleton of our own now. The rig is data, in the game's content: twenty-four joints with an adult's proportions, two builds, a stance, and the numbers a walk and a run are made from. As the C++ client starts, it builds each person's bones from the rig, and works out their motions into raylib's clips: the legs bend at the knee with two-bone inverse kinematics to reach where the feet go, so a foot that's down stays where it was put down, and the ground holds the body up as it dies. Mixamo's files and the Docker stage that converted them go, so a fresh clone draws everyone as a person. This is episode 60 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: MMORPG combat feel in C++ with hit-stop, knockback and a sword combo | nanoMMO Devlog
video:video.video:description: Our MMORPG's fights get some weight. The C++ server lets a skill land more than once, and each blow pushes the monster back over a fifth of a second, eased out, instead of moving it in one tick. The raylib client adds hit-stop on its own clock: each blow that lands holds the player and the monster still for a few frames, longer for a heavier hit, and they catch up after it, so the skill still ends when the server says. The monster lights up through the shader's emission and rocks back away from whoever hit it, the blade lights along its edge, cuts hang in the air with sounds made from code, and Space goes round a chain of three swings. This is episode 61 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: MMORPG sword skills in C++ that dash, launch and juggle | nanoMMO Devlog
video:video.video:description: Our MMORPG's sword gets five new skills. The C++ server can now move a player during a skill, along strides in the skills file, so that everyone sees a dash, and a blow can throw a monster into the air, keep it there with the next one and slam it down, for two seconds at most however many players take turns. Each monster's height goes to the raylib client, which tumbles it in the air, draws see-through copies of a player on a fast move, flashes the screen of the player using a skill and takes their camera in. Phantom Rush, Skyrend, Tempest Flurry, Cyclone and Severing Moon are entries in a text file, on a hotbar with a second row on Shift. This is episode 62 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: MMORPG game UI in C++ with a compass and a round minimap | nanoMMO Devlog
video:video.video:description: Our MMORPG's interface gets a look of its own, in the game's colours, with two fonts and panels with their corners cut, drawn over Dear ImGui and raylib in C++. It scales with the screen's height, from 720p to 4K, and a size the player sets. The menu bar goes: Escape closes what's open and then opens the game's menu, with the settings in pages. Your frame shows your face, rendered each frame, a compass along the top shows the monster you picked, the quests and the gates, and the minimap is round, zooms and can turn with the camera. This is episode 63 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: MMORPG drag and drop in C++ for the inventory and the hotbar | nanoMMO Devlog
video:video.video:description: The second half of our MMORPG's new interface, in C++ with Dear ImGui and raylib. The hotbar gets slots of brass in two rows, and a skill dragged onto another swaps with it, in an order the settings keep. The chat closes into a button that counts the lines since. Items drag as themselves, lit green or red by the server's own inventory rules, which the client now links as a library, and a move shows at once, before the server answers, and goes back if it says no. The character window becomes a paper doll, an item dropped over the world asks to be thrown away, and the login, the worlds, the characters, the loading and the death screens get the look. This is episode 64 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: From git clone to playing a C++ MMORPG | nanoMMO Devlog
video:video.video:description: We follow our own README on a brand-new Ubuntu machine, from git clone to a laptop playing on it across the network, and fix each thing that gets in the way. A doctor script checks the tools, libraries, Docker, ports and certificates, and prints one command that installs what's missing. The build loses its six hundred warnings, and Docker Compose stops publishing Redis and MySQL to the network. The servers find their files from any folder, a refused TLS handshake says what's wrong with the certificate and what to do, the certificates script adds the server's address, and a second world on one machine says its metrics port is taken. The steps end up on a getting started page, in the docs and on the website. This is episode 65 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: MMORPG guilds in C++, from MySQL to the nameplate | nanoMMO Devlog
video:video.video:description: Guilds for our MMORPG, in C++, MySQL and Redis. A guild changes for players other than the one who acts, so it lives in MySQL, a transaction for each change, with a unique key that keeps its name the world's once, whatever its case. A window on G founds one, and its name goes under yours, over your head. Officers and the leader ask players in, with an invitation that waits a minute in Redis (SET NX EX), or until they say no, so another guild can ask, and joining locks the guild's row first, so it can't fill up or end while you join. A chat for the guild alone goes out at once over TCP, in green, and when the leader leaves, the guild goes to whoever's been in it longest, or ends with the last one out. This is episode 66 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: MMORPG guild ranks in C++ with a roster, officers and kicks | nanoMMO Devlog
video:video.video:description: Guild ranks for our MMORPG, in C++ and MySQL. The guild window gets a roster, the highest rank first, with each player's level and who's playing now, which MySQL and the world put together and the server reads at most once a tick for each guild. A right-click on a player opens a menu of what your rank lets you do to theirs: the leader makes officers, a higher rank removes a lower one, and the leader can disband the guild after a question. Each change locks the guild's row first with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, then the player's, so a kick and a leave at the same moment from two instances of the world go one after the other without a deadlock, which a test runs on two MySQL connections. This is episode 67 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: Client-side prediction in a C++ MMORPG, on a slow network | nanoMMO Devlog
video:video.video:description: Client-side prediction for our MMORPG, in C++. On a network that netem slows to a 150 ms round trip, our player started and stopped walking late, as each key went to the server and back. The client now sends its keys each server tick, numbered, and the server applies them one a tick, catching up when some arrive late, and says which it applied last, with your place, which also puts the round trip on screen. The server's walking moves into a library the client links, built so that a step rounds alike on both, and the client walks you at once, puts you where the server has you after the last input it applied, walks you again through the rest, and fades what moved. Where the server moves you on its own, along a walk you asked for, up to a monster or with a skill, the client follows the server. This is episode 68 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: Smooth movement for other players in a C++ MMORPG | nanoMMO Devlog
video:video.video:description: Entity interpolation for our MMORPG, in C++. On a network that loses packets, the other players and the monsters stopped and lurched whenever a world from the server came late or not at all, as the client eased each of them towards the newest place it had. The client now keeps the last second of worlds, works out how far its clock is from the server's from the world that came quickest, and draws everyone else a tenth of a second in the past, between the two worlds on either side of that moment, while your own player stays in the present with last episode's prediction. When the next worlds are lost, the last two carry everyone on the way they were going, for a tenth of a second at most. This is episode 69 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: Sending only what changed in a C++ MMORPG | nanoMMO Devlog
video:video.video:description: Delta compression for our MMORPG's worlds, in C++. Each world from the server carried everyone near you in full, twenty times a second, so a player standing in a crowd cost as much as one walking through it. Each input now says the newest world the client has whole, the server remembers a second of what it sent each client as a hash of each player's and monster's piece, and anyone who hasn't changed since goes by their id alone, which the client keeps as it has them. The bots send their keys each tick, through a queue of writes, so they say which world they have often enough to help. With forty bots on one machine, measured from the server's Prometheus metrics, each gets roughly half the bytes it did. This is episode 70 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: Trying to cheat in my own C++ MMORPG | nanoMMO Devlog
video:video.video:description: Server-side anti-cheat for our MMORPG, in C++, by trying to cheat. The client runs on the player's machine, so anything it sends can be made up. So we write the server's red-team client: a player without a window that breaks the client's rules one at a time, and prints what it gets for it. More inputs than the server has ticks, a direction a thousand times too long or not a number, a swing at a monster twenty metres away and a skill sent ten times a tick all get nothing, as the server checks them against the world as it has it. Putting the sword in the bag as each blow lands, and back a moment later, cuts the swing short, for about twice the hits, so a skill now keeps the timings of the weapon it started with, and a decision record says why the server checks what a client asks for. This is episode 72 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: How MMO item dupes happen | nanoMMO Devlog
video:video.video:description: How item dupes happen in an MMORPG, and how the server stops them, in C++. Our red-team client learns to trade, with a partner that keeps the rules, and finds two dupes in last episode's simple trading. swap offers its sword, and once the partner's ready, moves it to another slot: the trade gives the copy it made at the offer and takes nothing, so two swords become three. run says it's ready and leaves at once, before the next tick saves the bags, and comes back to its old bag, sword and all. Now the server holds what's offered where it is, checks each place before it gives anything, has a ready name the revision of the trade it's for, and saves both players of a trade at once, in one Redis transaction with MULTI and EXEC, and a player as they leave. This is episode 75 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: Running my C++ MMORPG in a web browser with WebAssembly | nanoMMO Devlog
video:video.video:description: Our C++ MMORPG's client runs in a web browser, built as WebAssembly with Emscripten. A web CMake preset builds the client with Emscripten, with protoc built for the computer, as WebAssembly can't run there, and leaves out what needs sockets, which a page can't open. Then three things a browser does differently stop it on the way: a loop that never hands the browser its turn, shaders in desktop GLSL that WebGL 2 won't take, and reading a texture back in a format WebGL doesn't have. After those, the login screen draws in a tab. This is episode 76 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: Playing my C++ MMORPG offline in a browser, without a server | nanoMMO Devlog
video:video.video:description: Our C++ MMORPG plays offline: the client runs the world's rules on its own, from the library the server uses, so a browser starts straight into the world without a server. A local connection gives the client a world through the interface its network connection already has, at the server's tick, with the server's own code for inputs and for what a player is shown. In the browser, tall spindles stand by each person, which comes down to raylib sending WebGL its bone matrices untransposed, and a patch fixes it. This is episode 78 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: MMORPG PvP duels in C++ that end at one health | nanoMMO Devlog
video:video.video:description: Player versus player duels for our MMORPG, in C++. /duel and a name asks a player within ten metres, and once they say yes, in the chat or on the question on their screen, a flag goes down and the server counts three seconds down on both screens. Then each picks the other, as they would a monster, in a field of its own beside the monster's, which the world keeps for the opponent and nobody else, and swings and skills land on them. The blow that would leave a duellist without health leaves them one, and they've lost, as has anyone who goes more than 25 metres from the flag: nobody dies in a duel. The world keeps the duels, the server sends both sides each change over TCP, and the raylib client draws the countdown, the flag and a ring at the opponent's feet. This is episode 81 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: Weather effects and ambient sound in a C++ MMORPG | nanoMMO Devlog
video:video.video:description: Fire rain, snow, fireflies and the sound of the weather in our MMORPG, in C++ with raylib. The film tool gets the sky the server would send and a camera over a player's shoulder, and films thirteen quiet shots of the lands. Rain turns to snow above the snow line, ash and fire fall over the Ashlands' lava, the fire glowing past white so it blooms, and fireflies, wisps and lava sparks live in cells of the ground, so they stay put as the camera moves. The weather's sound is made from numbers, in loops folded so they go round without a seam and fed to an audio stream a buffer at a time, with thunder that comes after the flash at the speed of sound. The rain made from numbers sounded like glass beads, so the rain and the fire become recordings, kept out of git. This is episode 86 of a series about building an MMORPG from scratch in C++, with the focus on the engineering around the game.

video:video.video:title: nanoMMO, an MMORPG built from scratch in C++ (trailer)
video:video.video:description: nanoMMO is an MMORPG we're building from scratch in C++, client and server, one episode at a time. This is its trailer, filmed by the game itself: the client's own renderer draws every shot frame by frame, so the game's clock can run slower than the film's, and the slow motion, the sky and the sound are the game's. A series about building an MMORPG from scratch, with the focus on the engineering around the game.
